708.title: Gleaning (Ruth 2)
708.hook: Ruth gathers leftover grain, and Boaz tells his workers to drop some on purpose
708.howItsDone: Christians read Ruth 2 together with the gleaning laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and some churches and charities name food-rescue work, gathering surplus harvest for people in need, after gleaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naomi and whither thou goest, and your line was where you go, I go. Did you show up for the person you named, even in a small way? Day seven hundred eight.

Barley harvest in Bethlehem. Two widows have come home with no husbands and nothing to eat, and the younger one makes a plan. "Let me now go to the field, and glean ears of corn." Corn in the old English just means grain. To glean is to walk behind the reapers and pick up what they drop: the stray stalks, the bits at the edges. It's the work of people with nothing. So Ruth, a foreigner, goes out alone to somebody else's field. And the storyteller says, almost with a wink, "her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz," a relative of Naomi's dead husband. Her hap. It just happened. Then Boaz himself walks out from town and greets his workers, "The LORD be with you," and they answer, "The LORD bless thee."
screen: `LET ME NOW GO TO THE FIELD.`
`HER HAP WAS TO LIGHT ON BOAZ'S FIELD.`

segments.voice: Ruth isn't stealing, and she isn't begging. She's using a law. In Leviticus, God tells Israel: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest." Leave them, it says, for the poor and the stranger. Deuteronomy adds the sheaf you forgot in the field: don't go back for it; it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow. Ruth is two of those three at once. The law built a margin into every farm, so the hungry could feed themselves with their own hands. Boaz notices her and asks who she is. He tells her to stay in his field, near his young women, and says he's told the young men not to touch her. Ruth falls on her face and asks the question of the whole chapter: "Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger?" He's heard what she did for Naomi, he says, and he blesses her, under the God of Israel, "under whose wings thou art come to trust." Then comes the line this day turns on. When she gets up to glean, Boaz quietly tells his reapers: "let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her, and leave them, that she may glean them, and rebuke her not." The law said leave the edges and what drops. Boaz goes past the law: drop more, on purpose, and don't say a word. Ruth never has to ask for more. She simply finds more than she expected. That evening she beats out what she gathered, and the text says it was about an ephah of barley. Naomi sees it and asks where she worked. Hearing the name Boaz, the bitter widow from yesterday says, "Blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead."
screen: `THE LAW LEFT THE EDGES FOR STRANGERS.`
`WHY ME, SEEING I AM A STRANGER?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave something on purpose for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think through the rest of your day and look for the edges of your field: a little extra time, money, food, attention, a parking spot, the last slice. Pick one thing you could leave behind, quietly, for someone who could use it, in a way that lets them simply find it, the way Ruth found the handfuls. No speech, no credit. If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer as you decide. The bell holds the time.
Gleaning. Gathering what the reapers leave behind. The law left the edges of the field for the poor and the stranger, and Boaz left more.
Your line: drop some on purpose. Today, leave the thing you picked where someone can find it, and don't tell anyone it was you. Day seven hundred eight.

Boaz tells his reapers to drop extra grain on purpose
"let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her" (Ruth 2:16).

options: give her a sack of grain in front of everyone.
tell your reapers to drop handfuls for her on purpose, and say nothing.
follow the law, and leave the corners as usual.

what it means: a right the law gave the poor and the stranger, to the edges and the dropped grain of every field.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 19:9–10 and Deuteronomy 24:19 behind Ruth 2, and Boaz going past them with handfuls let fall on purpose (2:16).

709.title: Grandmother of a king (Ruth 4)
709.hook: an immigrant widow becomes great-grandmother of David, in Jesus' family tree
709.howItsDone: Christians read the end of Ruth together with Matthew 1, where Ruth is named in the family line of Jesus, as part of the story of how God's people came to include those from outside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gleaning, and your line was drop some on purpose. What did you leave behind for someone to find? Day seven hundred nine.

A man sits down at the city gate and waits. In this story the gate works like a courthouse, the place where business gets witnessed. Boaz is there because of a night that happened in between. In chapter three, Naomi sends Ruth to the threshing floor, and Ruth asks Boaz to spread his skirt over her, "for thou art a near kinsman." She's asking him to marry her, and to take up the family's cause. Boaz says yes, with one problem: there's a closer relative. So in the morning he sits at the gate, the closer relative walks by, and Boaz calls out, "Ho, such a one! turn aside, sit down here." The text never gives the man's name. Ten elders sit down to watch.
screen: `HO, SUCH A ONE! SIT DOWN HERE.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word for this relative is go'el, a redeemer: the near kinsman whose duty is to buy back family land and keep a dead man's name alive. Boaz lays it out. Naomi has a field to sell. Will you redeem it? The man says, I will. Then Boaz adds: the day you buy the field, you also take Ruth the Moabitess, the dead man's widow. The man backs out. "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance." He passes his shoe to Boaz, the old way of sealing a deal, and the man with no name walks out of the Bible. So Boaz marries Ruth, and they have a son. Now listen to who gets the last words. Not Boaz. Not Ruth. The women of the town, speaking to Naomi. Back in chapter one she said she came home empty. Now they tell her this child will restore her life and nourish her old age, "for thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons, hath born him." Better than seven sons, said of a foreign daughter-in-law. Naomi takes the boy and lays him in her bosom. The neighbors name him Obed. And then the book widens out in one sentence: "he is the father of Jesse, the father of David." The Moabite widow who gleaned in a stranger's field is the great-grandmother of Israel's king. The Gospel of Matthew opens with Jesus' family line, and there she is again: "Booz begat Obed of Ruth." The genealogy could have listed only fathers. It stops to say her name. Some readers take that line as a sign that the outsider was in the story all along, not added at the end.
screen: `THE MAN WITH NO NAME BACKS OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor an immigrant in your story. Settle, and breathe. Go back through your own line, or your town, your school, your work. Somewhere there's someone who came from somewhere else: a grandparent who crossed a border, a neighbor who learned your language, a coworker far from home, a person who married into the family and was never quite treated as family. Let one of them come to mind, by name if you can. Name one thing you have because they came. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
go'el, the Hebrew word for a redeemer: the near kinsman whose duty is to buy back family land and keep a dead man's name alive, as Boaz did for Ruth, great-grandmother of David.
Your line: the outsider in the line. Today, tell the person you named, or someone who knew them, one thing you have because they came. Day seven hundred nine.

710.title: Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 1)
710.hook: a woman prays so hard the priest thinks she's drunk
710.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Hannah's story when they pray about longing, infertility or grief, and read her silent prayer in 1 Samuel 1 alongside her song of thanks in 1 Samuel 2.

segments.voice: Yesterday, go'el, and your line was the outsider in the line. Who did you thank for coming, and what did you tell them? Day seven hundred ten.

"How long wilt thou be drunken? put away thy wine from thee." That's a priest, speaking to a woman at prayer. His name is Eli, and he's sitting on a seat by a post of the temple of the LORD at Shiloh, watching her. Her lips are moving. No sound is coming out. She's been there a long time. So he decides she's had too much at the family's meal and tells her to sober up. He couldn't be more wrong. A new book starts here, the first book of Samuel, and it doesn't open with a king or a battle. It opens with a woman who can't have children, a family trip to worship, and a prayer so deep it looks like a scandal.

Back up. Hannah's husband, Elkanah, has two wives. "Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children." Every year at Shiloh, the text says, her rival provoked her sore, to make her fret, until Hannah wept and couldn't eat. Elkanah loves her, and tries. "Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?" Yesterday the women of Bethlehem told Naomi that Ruth was better than seven sons, with the baby in Naomi's bosom. Here a husband asks if he's better than ten, and the text gives no answer from her. So Hannah gets up from the table and goes to pray. "She was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore." She makes a vow: if God will look on her affliction and remember her, and give her a son, she'll give him back to the LORD all the days of his life. Then the line that brings in Eli: "Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken." When he scolds her, she doesn't flinch. "No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD." Poured out. Like water from a jar, all of it, nothing kept back. Eli, to his credit, changes his mind at once: "Go in peace," he says, and may God grant your petition. And here's the detail to carry: Hannah goes and eats, and "her countenance was no more sad." She isn't pregnant yet. Nothing has changed. Only the jar is empty. Later she has a son and names him Samuel, saying, "Because I have asked him of the LORD." And she keeps her vow.
screen: `AM NOT I BETTER TO THEE THAN TEN SONS?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pour out your heart without words. Settle, and breathe. Let whatever's heaviest come up: the thing you want and don't have, the thing that keeps hurting. You don't need to say it, or even shape it into sentences. Hannah's voice wasn't heard. Let your breath carry it out, slowly, as if you were tipping a jar until it's empty. If you pray, you can do this before God. If you don't, simply let it out, and notice what's left when you're done. The bell holds the time.
Hannah's prayer. A silent prayer at Shiloh, so deep the priest thought she was drunk. She poured out her soul before the LORD, and went home no more sad.
Your line: poured out before the lord. Today, when the heavy thing comes back, don't argue with it. Pour it out once, silently, and then go and eat. Day seven hundred ten.

711.title: Speak, Lord (1 Samuel 3)
711.hook: a boy hears his name at night three times, and finally answers
711.carry: let none of his words fall to the ground
711.howItsDone: Some Christians use Samuel's words, speak, for thy servant heareth, before reading scripture or in quiet prayer, and read 1 Samuel 3 as a story about learning to recognize God's call.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah's prayer, and your line was poured out before the lord. When the heavy thing came back, did you pour it out, and then go and eat? Day seven hundred eleven.

"And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision." Precious here means rare. Heaven had gone quiet. Hannah's son Samuel is now a boy serving the old priest Eli at Shiloh, and one night he's lying down in the temple, where the ark of God is. The lamp of God hasn't gone out yet. Eli's eyes have grown so dim he can't see. Then a voice calls his name. The boy jumps up and runs to the old man. "Here am I; for thou calledst me." Eli says, I didn't call you. Lie down again. It happens a second time. Same run, same answer. It happens a third time.
screen: `THE LAMP OF GOD NOT YET OUT.`
`HERE AM I; FOR THOU CALLEDST ME.`

segments.voice: Why does Samuel keep running to the wrong room? The text answers plainly: "Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, neither was the word of the LORD yet revealed unto him." He isn't deaf, or foolish. He has simply never heard this voice before, so he takes it for the one voice he does know: Eli's. And here's the turn. On the third time, the old man who can barely see is the one who perceives it. "Eli perceived that the LORD had called the child." Eli hasn't restrained his own sons, and they're a scandal in the chapter before. But tonight he does the one thing a teacher can do. He gives the boy words: go lie down, and if he calls you, "thou shalt say, Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth." So Samuel lies down. Then the LORD comes and stands and calls as before: Samuel, Samuel. The boy answers, "Speak; for thy servant heareth." Listen closely and he leaves one word out. Eli told him to say Speak, LORD. Samuel only says Speak. Some readers have wondered why: nerves, or not yet knowing the name, or the text being careful. It doesn't say. What comes next is hard. The message is judgment on Eli's own house. In the morning Samuel is afraid to tell him. Eli insists, and when he hears it, the old man says only, "It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good." Then the chapter closes on the boy: the LORD was with him, and let none of his words fall to the ground. A quiet season ends with a child who learned to answer, from a man who knew he was being passed over.
screen: `SAMUEL DID NOT YET KNOW THE LORD.`
`A HARD WORD FOR ELI'S OWN HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer, and then listen. Settle, and breathe. Samuel kept answering the voice he already knew. For two minutes, set aside the usual voices in your head: the list, the worry, the old arguments. If you pray, you can say the boy's words once, quietly, "Speak; for thy servant heareth," and then stop talking. If you don't pray, simply say to yourself, I'm listening, and let the quiet stay quiet. Don't hunt for a message. Just practice being the one who hears. The bell holds the time.
Speak. The boy Samuel's answer in the night at Shiloh, after three calls and an old priest's help: speak; for thy servant heareth.
Your line: let none of his words fall to the ground. Today, in one conversation, stop running to answer and listen all the way to the end before you speak. Day seven hundred eleven.

712.title: Give us a king (1 Samuel 8)
712.hook: the people want a king like everyone else, and are warned what kings take
712.howItsDone: Christians read 1 Samuel 8 in different ways, as a warning about power and as part of the long road to King David, and some read it when thinking about how much to borrow from the culture around them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy at Shiloh answered, and your line was let none of his words fall to the ground. In one conversation, did you listen all the way to the end? Day seven hundred twelve.
screen: `LET NONE OF HIS WORDS FALL TO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Time has run on. The boy who answered in the night is now an old man, and the story repeats itself in a way that stings. Samuel makes his sons judges, and "his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment." Eli's sons all over again. So the elders of Israel come to Samuel at Ramah with a request that sounds perfectly reasonable: you're old, your sons aren't like you, "now make us a king to judge us like all the nations." And the text says, simply, "the thing displeased Samuel."
screen: `HIS SONS WALKED NOT IN HIS WAYS.`

segments.voice: Samuel takes it personally. So he prays, and God's answer is surprising twice over. First: give them what they ask. "Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them." It isn't about you, Samuel. Second: but warn them first. Tell them what a king is like. So Samuel stands up and gives a blunt speech, and its key word is take. "He will take your sons." For his chariots, his horsemen, his fields, his weapons. "He will take your daughters to be confectionaries, and to be cooks, and to be bakers." He'll take your best fields and vineyards and give them to his servants. He'll take a tenth of your grain, a tenth of your flocks, your servants, your donkeys. "And ye shall be his servants." And one day you'll cry out because of the king you chose. Then the people answer, and they don't argue with a single point. "Nay; but we will have a king over us; That we also may be like all the nations; and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles." Like all the nations, again. They heard every cost and still chose to belong. God tells Samuel, make them a king. Readers don't agree on how to hear this chapter. Some hear a warning against kingship itself, or against any power that only takes. Others point out that Deuteronomy had already allowed for a king, and that the trouble was the reason: to be like everyone else. Christian readers also follow this road on to David and a promised throne, and to Jesus called the son of David. The chapter itself just ends with the request granted, and the warning on the record.
screen: `NAY; BUT WE WILL HAVE A KING.`
`READERS HEAR IT MORE THAN ONE WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice when you want to be like everyone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you want right now mostly because others have it: a phone, a look, a kind of house, a way of talking, a stance online. Don't judge it yet. Just ask Samuel's question: what will it take? Your time, your money, your attention, your quiet. Let the list come, the way his did. If you pray, you can bring that wanting to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Ramah. The town where Israel's elders came to Samuel and asked for a king to judge and lead them like all the nations, after hearing everything a king would take.
Your line: not like the nations. Today, before you buy, post or say something because everyone does, stop and count what it will take. Day seven hundred twelve.

713.title: Hiding among the baggage (1 Samuel 10:17–24)
713.hook: chosen as king, tall Saul hides among the luggage
713.tomorrow: The Lord looks on the heart
713.howItsDone: Christians read Saul's hiding as a very human moment at the start of a story that ends in tragedy, and preachers sometimes use it to talk about the fear that comes with being called.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at Ramah, the elders said give us a king, and your line was not like the nations. What did you almost do because everyone does, and what would it have taken? Day seven hundred thirteen.

The whole nation is gathered at Mizpeh to find out who their king will be, and they're choosing by lot. Tribe by tribe, the lot narrows. The tribe of Benjamin is taken. Then one family in Benjamin. Then one man: Saul, the son of Kish. Every head turns. And the text says, "when they sought him, he could not be found." The king is missing from his own coronation. So they enquire of the LORD further: where is he? And the answer comes back, in the King James words: "Behold, he hath hid himself among the stuff."

The stuff is the baggage: the gear and supplies people brought to the gathering. Somewhere behind the packs and the bundles, the new king is crouching. And he's not easy to hide. When they run and fetch him and he stands up, "he was higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward." Taller than everyone, folded up behind the luggage. Why hide? The story has already given clues. In the chapter before, Saul was out looking for his father's lost donkeys when he met Samuel. Samuel told him the desire of all Israel was on him, and Saul answered, "Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel?" Then Samuel anointed him in private with a vial of oil. So when the lot falls today, Saul has already been anointed, and he hides anyway. Fear, modesty, dread of the weight: the text doesn't say which, and readers have heard all three. Then Samuel presents him to the crowd. "See ye him whom the LORD hath chosen, that there is none like him among all the people?" And the people shout, "God save the king." One more detail, just past today's verses. Not everyone cheers. Some say, how shall this man save us, and they despise him and bring him no gifts. "But he held his peace." The man who hid in the baggage stays quiet under contempt. Some readers who know how Saul's story ends come back to this chapter, to the tall, frightened man behind the bags, before anything went wrong.
screen: `THE STUFF: THE GEAR AND THE BAGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: step out from behind something. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself where you're hiding among the stuff right now. A role you've been asked to take and keep dodging. A conversation you know is yours to have. A gift you keep tucked behind busyness, or other people, or being too tired. Let one come to mind. You don't have to step out yet. Just picture standing up from behind the bags, all the way up. If you pray, you can ask for courage to be found. The bell holds the time.
Mizpeh. The gathering place where Saul, chosen by lot, hid himself among the stuff, and had to be fetched out to stand before the people.
Your line: come out from the baggage. Today, take one step toward the thing you named: say yes, send the message, raise your hand. Day seven hundred thirteen.

screen: `DAY 713 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LORD LOOKS ON THE HEART.`

714.title: The Lord looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:1–13)
714.hook: the youngest son, out with the sheep, is chosen and anointed
714.howItsDone: Christians read 1 Samuel 16:7 as a reminder that God does not judge by appearance, and read the anointing of the youngest son alongside other stories in scripture where God chooses the overlooked.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at Mizpeh, Saul hid among the baggage, and your line was come out from the baggage. Did you take one step out from behind something? Day seven hundred fourteen.

An old prophet is grieving, and God tells him to stop. "How long wilt thou mourn for Saul, seeing I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? fill thine horn with oil, and go." The tall king from yesterday has gone wrong, and Samuel can't let go of him. Now he's sent to Bethlehem, Ruth's town, to a man named Jesse. Earlier this week we met his family: Jesse is the grandson of Ruth and Boaz. Samuel is afraid. "How can I go? if Saul hear it, he will kill me." So he goes quietly, with a heifer for a sacrifice, and invites Jesse and his sons. One of them is about to be anointed king. Samuel doesn't know which.
screen: `HOW LONG WILT THOU MOURN FOR SAUL?`

segments.voice: Jesse's son Eliab walks in first, and Samuel thinks he's found him. "Surely the LORD'S anointed is before him." And God answers with the line that names today: "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." Height of his stature. Yesterday the crowd cheered a king who stood taller than everyone from the shoulders up. Samuel is about to be drawn by height again, and God stops him. So the sons pass by, one after another. Each time, the same answer. The text sums it up: "Jesse made seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. And Samuel said unto Jesse, The LORD hath not chosen these." Then the question: "Are here all thy children?" And Jesse admits, "There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep." Nobody thought to call him in. Samuel says, we will not sit down till he comes. Notice something: until now, the story hasn't even said his name. He's just the youngest, the one with the sheep. He arrives, and the text, with a little smile, describes him anyway: "ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to." The point was never that looks are bad. It's that they aren't what God goes by. "Arise, anoint him: for this is he." Samuel pours the oil in front of his brothers, and only then does the name appear: "the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward." Then Samuel rises and goes home to Ramah. Nothing in these verses makes the boy king yet.
screen: `SURELY THE LORD'S ANOINTED IS BEFORE HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look past someone's appearance. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you've sized up by the outside: their clothes, their age, their size, their accent, their job, the way they talk. Someone you'd have left out with the sheep. Hold their face in mind for a moment, then try to look past it. What do you actually know of their heart? What might be there that you haven't seen? If you pray, you can ask to see them the way the text says God sees. The bell holds the time.
Eliab. Jesse's eldest son, whom Samuel almost anointed before God said, man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
Your line: god looks on the heart. Today, give the person you named one more look, a real conversation or a real question, past the outside. Day seven hundred fourteen.

myth: Samuel recognized David as the chosen one right away
he thought it was Eliab, until God told him to look not on his countenance (16:6–7).

fork.setup: you're Samuel. seven of Jesse's sons have passed by you, and God has said no to each. what do you do?
options: choose the best of the seven anyway.
ask, are here all thy children?
go home and tell God there's no one.
fork.reveal: Jesse admits there's one more, the youngest, out with the sheep. Samuel won't sit down till he comes (16:11).

original.note: Hebrew: heart. the LORD looketh on the heart, 1 Samuel 16:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: God picks the little guy, and looks don't matter.
what it means: Samuel is drawn by height again, and God stops him: the LORD looketh on the heart.
what a scholar hears: 'the height of his stature' (16:7) echoing Saul's shoulders and upward (10:23), and David's name withheld until 16:13.
